There's always a comeback in life, and there's always a comeback in fencing." Listen on the FIE's YouTube channel.

items.headline: By the Book: You Can't Appeal What the Referee Saw
items.body: A referee's ruling on what happened on the strip, like whether a hit landed or a fencer stepped off the side, is a "point of fact," and it can't be appealed (t.172). Argue a point of fact during the bout, or make an appeal the Head Referee finds unjustified (t.174), and it's a First Group offense: a yellow card the first time, then a red card (a penalty touch) for each repeat in that bout (t.165). Appeal the rule, not the call.

items.body:
*Editor's note: The fencer in this story is the editor's son.*

The light went on, and the argument started. In a pool bout at a national tournament two years ago, an Elite FC fencer's opponent scored a touch that, the fencer's family says, landed off the strip. The fencer said the blade never hit him.

By the family's account, the opponent waved a hand to signal no touch, the Elite FC coach pointed that out on the spot, and neither the opponent's coach nor family said a word in the touch's defense. The only person who thought it was a touch, the family says, was the referee, who said she thought she saw it hit. The fencer made a formal appeal, and the Head Referee came over and ruled that it was the referee's call. Pools had no video replay. The fencer lost the bout by one touch.

On paper, a hit that misses the fencer shouldn't count. In epee, touches "made on the ground where it is not insulated" are disregarded (t.93), and a touch that lands on the strip and registers is annulled (t.94.1). The catch is who decides whether it landed. That is a "point of fact," and against a point of fact "no appeal can be made" (t.172.1). An appeal can challenge only how a rule was applied, and the Head Referee settles it (t.172.2, t.174). No rule we found gives an opponent's signal any formal weight.

**Both sides (opinion).** For the call: the referee judges from where she stands, and making her view final keeps bouts from being re-argued touch by touch. Against it: when the fencer who scored signals a miss, a referee who only thought she saw a hit has a thin basis for a decisive touch.

**The verdict: judgment call.** On the family's own account, the Head Referee applied the rules correctly. A referee's view of a hit can't be appealed, no matter how differently it looked from the side of the strip.

**For parents,** the lesson is narrow but useful. You can't appeal what a referee saw, only how a rule was applied. Only the fencer can appeal, and it has to happen right away, before the next touch. At national tournaments today, video replay is guaranteed only in later direct-elimination rounds (from the round of 16 or 8, depending on the event), not in pools. And a parent's phone video doesn't count.

items.headline: Vet Worlds, Part Two: Two World Titles for U.S. Women
items.body:
The U.S. women's epee veterans left the Veteran World Championships in Tbilisi, Georgia, with two world titles and four individual medals.

Leslie Marx led the way in Veteran 50, working through an 83-fencer field and beating Belgium's Nathalie Vandewalle 10-4 in the final. The FIE says it was her first title in the event since 2017.

The Veteran 40 gold came down to one touch. Cassandra Bates lost the final 10-9 to Julia Ashchuk and took silver, and Lacey Biniak, who fell to Ashchuk 10-8 in the semifinals, took bronze. That gave the U.S. two of the four medals in a 63-fencer field. In Veteran 70, Charlotta Bowie won bronze after a 10-7 semifinal loss to Germany's Astrid Kircheis, the eventual champion.

Then came the team event. In a field of 19 teams, the U.S. beat Italy 45-40 in the semifinals and France 45-31 in the final for gold.

The championships, held Oct. 9–17, drew 1,273 athletes from 65 nations. The women's epee events ran Oct. 12–14.

items.headline: For the Parents: Qualifying Isn't Registering
items.body: Qualifying isn't the same as registering. A fencer who earns a Junior Olympics spot, including through a division qualifier, still has to sign up; USA Fencing says it does not register anyone automatically. Register by the Nov. 11 regular-fee deadline, even if a fencer's qualifier comes later; the entry stays "pending" until qualification is confirmed. Division results can take two to five days to reach USA Fencing. The 2027 Junior Olympics run Jan. 8–11 in Oklahoma City.

items.headline: After the Split: What Fencers Said
items.body: After October's NAC, the first with fields split into Elite and Challenger, r/Fencing compared notes. The top-voted take came from a fan of the change: top fencers used to get easy pools and early DEs, and now they meet strong opponents every round. One fencer placed in Elite called it the most concentrated U.S. event they'd seen. Another put it simply: "Pools was tough but it was a lot more fun." Not everyone was sold. One poster said coaches found the day brutal, for them and for referees, and another argued the tiers reflect how active a fencer is more than how strong. Others said it's too early to judge from one event, and several want the 20% pool cut dropped in Challenger.
items.fact_check_line: *Fact check:* Fields are set by Unified Points List rank 15 days out. In Cadet, an Elite top-64 finish (51.6 points) outscores a Challenger top-16 finish (49.2).

items.headline: Photo from History: 1965: Club epee, with everyone close enough to watch
items.body: The Oude RAI in Amsterdam was the setting for the Dutch national team epee championship on 21 November 1965. In this photograph, Laurens van Tiggele is at left and Raoul Popken at right; the archive records Zaal Abrahamse of The Hague as the winning club. Around their exchange, the hall is busy: a spectator sits close behind them, another bout continues in the background, and a body cord trails from the nearest fencer. The tight framing keeps all of that activity together, with the two masked opponents in the foreground and the people watching and competing close behind them.
items.caption: Laurens van Tiggele, left, faces Raoul Popken at the Dutch national team epee championship in Amsterdam’s Oude RAI on 21 November 1965. The winning club was Zaal Abrahamse of The Hague; spectators and another bout fill the space behind the two fencers.
items.credit: Photo: unknown photographer / Anefo, Nationaal Archief, collection 2.24.01.05, no. 918-4711 (Nov. 21, 1965). CC0 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/). Full-resolution JPEG converted from the archive’s original TIFF. Cropped. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Duel_tussen_Van_Tiggele_(links)_en_Popken,_Bestanddeelnr_918-4711.jpg.
